note: Read 2026-11-01 at the owner's word ("Continue on to the rest of layer 4"): the figures that decide which parts are written for an actor or an actress (how breakdowns name a part's gender and ethnicity, a part's playing age and language) and the acting awards' categories by sex. One research subagent; every quote checked by the lead against its saved page. The Academy's rules are read from a copy (oscars.org refused this environment); KEEP entry 4's line holds: published practice only, never an ability. The shares of parts by gender, age and ethnicity (the screen's studies, in the US, the UK, Australia and Canada, and the breakdowns' counts of 2006 and 2017), and the blockers for Canada's and the Geena Davis Institute's shares, were removed on 2026-11-04 with the sources only they cited: casting's breakdowns drew parts at those shares, and casting went that day (the owner: "there is no casting because we're going to be in our own film"). Sowa's 2017 count stays for its categories alone, which the parts the life's productions write still use.

figures.finding: Of 3,714 character breakdowns for 269 SAG-AFTRA television shows (January to August 2017), each was written for men, for women, open gender (open to either a man or a woman) or genderqueer or non-binary.
figures.applies: US scripted English-language television (broadcast, cable, streaming), breakdowns distributed January-August 2017.
figures.use: A part is written for men, women, either (open gender) or a non-binary performer, the categories breakdowns use; its shares aren't read, the life's own production writing its parts.

sources.said: Figure 1 shows the gender distribution in the Breakdowns as Men 57.6% (n = 2,141), Women 37.9% (n = 1,408), Open Gender
Open Gender means casting is open to either a man or woman in the role.

figures.finding: Spotlight (UK) requires every performer to list a playing age range; it warns when the range is more than 15 years wide, suggests the actual age plus and minus five years as a rule of thumb, and keeps a young performer's range tight (e.g. 9-11 at ten).
figures.applies: Spotlight performer profiles (UK and Ireland casting platform), as published in 2026.
figures.use: The player's playing age is a range around the real age (default five years either side, at most fifteen wide, narrow for a child), and a part is open to the player when its age band overlaps that range.

sources.said: Your playing age means the range of ages that you can convincingly play as an actor and is mandatory information that must be on your Spotlight profile.
A warning message will appear if you select ages more than 15 years apart.
If you’re unsure what your playing age is, it’s recommended that you add and subtract five years from your actual age. For instance, if you’re 25, your playing age could be between 20 and 30.
Generally, it will sit tightly either side of their actual age, e.g. If they’re ten, it would be ‘9-11’.

figures.finding: Equity (UK) advises that performers should not be asked their age, ethnicity and other protected characteristics in a casting, except actual age when casting children or age-restricted advertising; a performer asked their age may give their playing range.
figures.applies: UK castings, auditions and interviews (Equality Act 2010; Equity's casting questions card and Casting Manifesto with Spotlight, CDG and PMA).
figures.use: In UK castings the game reads the player's playing range, never the real age, except for a child performer or an age-restricted advertisement.

sources.said: If asked about age, for example, you could say: "My playing range is..." Or "Equity advises me not to answer that"

Performers must not be asked for personal information, verbally or in writing prior to or during the audition process. This includes but is not limited to address, personal phone numbers, ethnicity and age except where actual age can and must be identified when casting children and in relation to casting for age restricted products in advertising.

figures.finding: Of 3,714 US television breakdowns (2017), some said 'open ethnicity' (please submit all ethnicities), some gave none, and the rest named one of White, Black, Latina/o, Asian, Middle Eastern, Indian/South East Asian, Mixed Race/Biracial, Pacific Islander and Native American.
figures.applies: US scripted English-language television breakdowns (Breakdown Services), January-August 2017.
figures.use: A part names one of these ethnicities, or none; only a part that names one reads the person's race or ethnicity. The shares aren't read, the life's own production writing its parts.

sources.said: Figure 2 shows the race/ethnicity of the Breakdowns as White 15.5% (n = 577), Black 8.5% (n = 316), Asian 3.8% (n = 144), Indian/South East Asian 1.5% (n = 59), Latina/o 8.3% (n = 309), Native American 0.5% (n = 20), Middle Eastern 1.6% (n = 62), Pacific Islander 0.7% (n = 28), Mixed Race/Biracial 1.4% (n = 52), No Ethnicity Given 30% (n = 1,115), Open Ethnicity
Open Ethnicity refers to a note in some Breakdowns that say “please submit all ethnicities.”
34.3% of Breakdowns for female characters stated “open ethnicity” (n = 483).

figures.finding: Every project on Breakdown Services carries a standard statement asking agents to submit performers without regard to race, ethnicity, age and other protected bases 'unless otherwise specifically indicated'; many breakdowns still specify race or ethnicity.
figures.applies: US breakdowns distributed by Breakdown Services (Breakdown Express, Actors Access), as observed 2017.
figures.use: The default for a part is open to every ethnicity; a part reads the player's race or ethnicity only where its breakdown names one.

sources.said: Paradoxically, every project listed in the Breakdowns includes the following statement: “We are committed to diverse, inclusive casting. For every role, please submit qualified performers, without regard to disability, race and ethnicity, age, color, national origin, or any other basis prohibited by law unless otherwise specifically indicated.” That said, many Breakdowns clearly do specify the race/ethnicity, age, gender, and so forth, of a role.

figures.finding: Published practice in the UK: performers must not be asked their ethnicity in a casting, and the Equity Casting Manifesto (with Spotlight, the CDG and the PMA) asks that an advertised breakdown be presented in the most inclusive way possible; in Canadian advertising the CMA asks a casting to say if it is open to all ethnicities and to list the ethnicities wanted rather than 'ethnically ambiguous'.

value.canada_advertising_rule: say if open to all ethnicities; list specific ethnicities

figures.applies: UK castings (Equity and Spotlight, 2026); Canadian advertising castings (Canadian Marketing Association DEI Committee, May 2023).
figures.use: Nobody in a casting asks the player's ethnicity; a breakdown that names an ethnicity is matched against the player's own optional field, and the game never infers it.

sources.said: Where roles are advertised, the casting breakdown should be presented in the most inclusive way possible.

In line with the law and with specific exceptions, performers should not be asked for personal information, verbally or in writing, as part of the audition. This includes actual age, ethnicity, disability, pregnancy, marital/civil partnership status or sexual orientation.
Specify if the casting is open to all ethnicities. List all who may attend rather than being generic.
Keep age as broad as possible, e.g., adult, child or looks like 40-70 year-old.

figures.finding: Of 8,798 films released in North American cinemas 2003-2017, 81.4% featured English as a main language and 31% had more than one language; French featured in 12%, Spanish 8.6%, German 5.2%, Hindi 4.9% (a film counts if it has at least a line in the language).
figures.applies: Films released in North American cinemas, 2003-2017; counts films, not roles.
figures.use: A film in the North American market has a second language about three times in ten; only such a film can write a part asking a language other than English. The share of parts (not films) is not published (see blockers).

sources.said: Across those 8,798 movies studied, 81.4% featured English as one of their main languages. Other popular languages included French (featured in 12% of movies), Spanish (8.6%), German, (5.2%) and Hindi (4.9%).
Films can have more than one language, and indeed, 31% of the films in my study did.

figures.finding: The main US television breakdowns distributed to Los Angeles and New York agents are English-language; Spanish-language network characters (Telemundo) were not in them in 2017.
figures.applies: US SAG-AFTRA television breakdowns, 2017.
figures.use: A US market part assumes English; a part in another language belongs to that language's market and reads the player's languages.

sources.said: This study examines English language television shows. While Telemundo is in negotiations with SAG-AFTRA (McNary, 2018), Telemundo characters are not currently included in the main Breakdowns distributed to LA and NY agents and managers.
